topics.title: New Formula???
topics.text:
A classic problem: if you roll a die 2 times what is the probability that you don't get a six. That is just 1-(5/6)^2

and in general if you roll it P times you get 1-(5/6)^P. I was wondering if there was any pattern to this as P got bigger, I did a lot of tedious work and finally saw a pattern. I exploited that pattern and came up with a formula for something a lot more general: 1-(k/n)^P

Formula$\frac{(n+k)^{P-1}-\sum_{a=0}^{P-1} ((\binom{P-1}{a}-1)n^{P-(a+1)}k^{a})}{n^P} = 1-\left(\frac{k}{n}\right)^{P}$

Here is what the formula is:https://docs.google.com/document/d/1l7T352YBlccXaKkuvCceRnRV7hnzqiAaXqeMuKmEsNY/edit?usp=sharing


Before you check what I got try to do it and then see if you have what I have, also tell me if something is wrong.

Thanks :D

topics.title: Astonishing Probabilities
topics.text:
In the city of Townsville, population $10000$, each person has a $1$ percent chance of having a certain disease. To determine whether someone does or does not have it, they take a test which predicts with $98$ percent accuracy whether or not they have the disease if they DON'T have it and predicts with $97$ percent accuracy whether or not they have the disease if they DO have it. If I am tested for the disease and the test reads positive (meaning it says I have the disease), what is the actual probability I have it?

Read the question carefully.

SolutionRemarkably, the chance I have the disease is about $33$ percent



Out of 10000 people, 1 percent have the disease, meaning 100 people have the disease.

Of those 100 people, the test reads on average positive for 97 people and negative for 3 people.

Of the 9900 who don't have the disease, 98 percent, (9702 people) take the test and it reads negative, and for 198 people (the margin of error for the test), it reads positive even though they don't have the disease.

Thus, the are a total of 198+97 people for which the test reads positive. And there are only 97 people for which the test reads positive and they DO have the disease.

Probability = $\frac{97}{198+97}$ = $\frac{97}{295}$

That is about $32$ percent.



A lengthier explanation to better understand the problem:



Amount of people who have the disease = $1$ percent of $10000$ which is $100$

Out of those $100$ people, the test reads positive for $97$ percent, which is $97$ people.



Amount of people who don't have the disease = $99$ percent of $10000$, which is $9900$

Out of those, the test reads positive for $98$ percent of the people, which is $9702$ people. This leaves $198$ people for which the test reads positive even though they are healthy.

The total number of people for which the test reads positive is $97 + 198$, which is $295$ ($97$ from the unhealthy population, and $198$ from the healthy population.)

Out of those $295$ people, only $97$ are unhealthy, rendering a probability of $\frac{97}{295}$, which is roughly $33$ percent.

This percentage decreases as the population increases. (It is less than 5 percent for one million people!)

topics.title: k My 3 reasons for why 0.99... = 1 so 5th graders know why!!!
topics.text:
Why is it that $0.99\ldots = 1$?



These are 3 reasons with only using Pre-algebra or lower work.



Reason 1First, let $x = 0.99\ldots$

Next, let's multiply 10 to both sides.

$10x=9.99\ldots$

subtract x to both sides and get,

$9x=9$

Then, divide 9 to both sides and get

$x=1$




Reason 2Since we know that $\frac{1}{3} = 0.33\ldots$,

we multiply 3 on both sides to get,

$\frac{3}{3} = 0.99\ldots$

and since $\frac{3}{3} = 1$,

we know that $1 = 0.99\ldots$




Reason 3Let's subtract $0.99\ldots$ from 1.

We get:

$ 1.00000000\ldots$

$-0.99999999\ldots$

__________

$0.00000000\ldots$

and we never ever reach something greater than 0, so we know that $1=0.99\ldots$
